title: School finances 2: Money in a no-fee public school
description: How a public school becomes no-fee, how the state allocation may be spent, what section 21 status means, voluntary fundraising, and the budget, reporting and audit duties that still apply.

lessons.title: What makes a school no-fee
lessons.summary: National quintiles, the no fee threshold and the annual lists that decide which public schools may not charge fees.
lessons.body:
## 🎯 Why it matters

A no-fee school may not charge compulsory school fees, so almost all its money comes from the State. Governors need to know how that status is decided, what it guarantees and what it does not. This module covers public schools only. Independent schools set fees under their own constitution and parent contracts, even if they receive a state subsidy.

## 📜 The legal building blocks

- The Minister must determine national quintiles for public schools and national norms and standards for school funding (SASA s35(1)). The norms in use are the Amended National Norms and Standards for School Funding, Government Notice 869 in Government Gazette 29179 of 31 August 2006, as updated by later notices. This lesson calls them "the norms".
- The norms must place learners and schools into five national quintiles according to financial means, with quintile 1 the poorest (SASA s35(2)).
- Each year the Minister must, by notice in the Government Gazette, determine the quintiles, or parts of quintiles, that the MEC must use to identify schools that may not charge fees (SASA s39(7)).

## 🔢 The two tests

Under the norms, a school is a no-fee school only if both of these apply (norms para 156):

1. The school is in a quintile, or part of a quintile, that the Minister has identified under s39(7).
2. The school receives a per learner allocation at least equal to the "no fee threshold" for that year.

The no fee threshold is the level of funding per learner, set in the norms, that allows a school to be declared no-fee (SASA s1). The Minister may make the s39(7) determination only if funding of at least the threshold has been secured (SASA s39(8)).

In recent years the Minister's determination has covered schools in quintiles 1 to 3. For example, the 2014 amendment to the norms (Government Notice 12, Gazette 37230 of 17 January 2014) determined all learners in quintiles 1 to 3 to be in no fee schools for 2014, and set the no fee threshold for 2014 at R1,059 per learner. Amounts change every year.

> 💡 Tip: Never quote last year's per learner amount to parents. Ask the district for your school's allocation letter and the current national targets notice.

## 📋 Who draws up the list

1. The MEC identifies and lists the qualifying schools in the province (SASA s39(9)).
2. The Minister checks the list against the quintile determination and publishes it per province in the Government Gazette (SASA s39(10)).
3. The MEC may, after consulting the governing bodies, declare additional schools no-fee by notice in the Provincial Gazette. These must be the poorest schools in the province outside the national list, and only if the province has secured funding of at least the no fee threshold (SASA s39(13) to (16)).

This is how some quintile 4 or 5 schools in poorer areas become no-fee.

## ⚠️ If the money falls short

If a no-fee school receives less than the no fee threshold from the provincial department, it may charge school fees, but only up to the difference between the threshold and what it actually received (SASA s39(11) and (12); norms para 163). The norms say the "received" amount includes both money transferred and the value of goods the department bought on the school's behalf.

> ⚠️ Watch out: This is a narrow exception, not a licence to bring back fees. Get the shortfall confirmed in writing by the district first, and the normal parents' meeting and exemption rules would still apply.

## ✅ Key points

- The Minister sets national quintiles and the funding norms (SASA s35).
- A school is no-fee if it is in a quintile identified by the Minister and receives at least the no fee threshold per learner (SASA s39(7) and (8); norms para 156).
- The Minister publishes the national list, and the MEC may add the poorest remaining schools if funded (SASA s39(10) and (13)).
- A school that receives less than the threshold may charge only the shortfall (SASA s39(11) and (12)).

lessons.title: The state allocation and how it may be spent
lessons.summary: What the per learner school allocation is for, the spending categories in the norms, and what it may never pay for.
lessons.body:
## 💡 What the allocation is

The State must fund public schools from public revenue on an equitable basis, and must tell schools each year enough about that funding to let them budget (SASA s34). Under the norms, the "school allocation" is a per learner amount that rises as the quintile gets poorer, so a quintile 1 school receives more per learner than a quintile 5 school.

> 💡 Tip: Your allocation letter from the provincial department is the most important finance document of the year. File it with the budget and quote its figures at the parents' meeting.

## 🎯 What it is meant to cover

The norms say the allocation is intended for non-personnel recurrent items, small capital items and normal repairs and maintenance of the school's physical infrastructure, and is intended only for promoting efficient and quality education in public ordinary schools (norms para 95).

## 🗂️ The six categories in the norms

The norms give examples, not a closed list, in these categories (norms para 96):

1. **Learning support materials**: textbooks, library books, science equipment, computers and software, learner desks and chairs.
2. **Non-learning-support equipment**: other furniture, copiers, telephones, connectivity equipment, cleaning equipment, first aid kits, sports equipment.
3. **Educational consumables**: for example learner stationery.
4. **Non-educational consumables**: office stationery, cleaning materials, fuel.
5. **Repairs and maintenance services**: building repairs, equipment repairs, light bulbs.
6. **Other services**: electricity, water, rates, telephone, internet, audit fees, bank charges, legal services, security, transport, insurance.

The norms link categories 1 to 4 to the SASA s21(1)(c) function, category 5 to s21(1)(a) and category 6 to s21(1)(d) (norms para 96). Lesson 3 explains those functions.

## 🚫 What it may NOT pay for

The school allocation may not be used to pay for personnel or new buildings (norms para 99). So the allocation cannot pay an SGB-employed assistant teacher or build a new classroom block. Such costs must come from other sources, such as fundraising or donations, and any staff the SGB employs must be affordable from those sources.

## ⚖️ The recommended breakdown

- Each provincial department must give every school a recommended breakdown of its allocation across the s21 functions and the categories above, in the official allocation letter (norms para 115).
- Provinces may add further conditions, which must also be in that letter (norms para 116).
- Schools must be guided by the breakdown. A school that wants to under-budget for educational items compared with the breakdown should do so only after consulting the department and getting its approval (norms para 140).
- Where educational inputs suffer because of large deviations, the department should seriously consider withdrawing s21 functions under SASA s22 (norms para 140).

> ⚠️ Watch out: Some provinces set percentage splits in their allocation letters or circulars (for example a minimum share for learning materials). These differ by province and year. Follow the letter you received, and check the current circular with your district office.

## 🧯 Emergencies

The governing body may use the allocation for urgent needs such as storm damage, if it is in the interests of education and follows the policy on the allocation. The province may run a reimbursement system for this, but schools have no automatic right to be refunded (norms para 98).

## ✅ Key points

- The allocation is per learner and pro-poor, set under the norms made in terms of SASA s35.
- It covers non-personnel recurrent costs, small capital items and repairs and maintenance (norms para 95).
- It may never pay for personnel or new buildings (norms para 99).
- Follow the province's recommended breakdown and get approval before under-spending on educational items (norms paras 115 and 140).

lessons.title: Section 21 functions: who buys what
lessons.summary: How section 21 status decides whether the school or the department buys textbooks, pays for services and does maintenance.
lessons.body:
## 🧩 The allocated functions

A governing body may apply in writing to the Head of Department (HOD) to be allocated extra functions (SASA s21(1)). The three that involve spending the allocation are:

- **s21(1)(a)**: to maintain and improve the school's property, buildings and grounds, including hostels.
- **s21(1)(c)**: to purchase textbooks, educational materials or equipment.
- **s21(1)(d)**: to pay for services to the school.

The HOD may refuse only if the governing body lacks the capacity to perform the function effectively, may attach conditions, and must give written reasons (SASA s21(2) to (4)). A refusal may be appealed to the MEC (SASA s21(5)). The MEC may also grant functions to some governing bodies by notice in the Provincial Gazette without an application (SASA s21(6)).

> 💡 Tip: Being no-fee and being a section 21 school are different things. A no-fee school can have all, some or none of these functions. Check your status on the province's list of section 21 status, which the norms require each province to keep (norms para 130).

## 💸 Section 21 schools: the money comes to you

A school allocated one or more of these functions receives a transfer into its school fund for those functions, with a recommended breakdown (norms para 132). It may do its own procurement and deal directly with suppliers, following standard procurement procedures, the HOD's financial directives under SASA s37 and any provincial conditions (norms para 133). It must keep documents that prove correct dealing with suppliers and records of how goods and services were used, and produce them for officials and auditors (norms para 133).

## 📦 Non-section 21 schools: the department buys

Where the functions have not been allocated, the department commonly buys goods for the school in bulk up to the value of the allocation and manages delivery (norms para 135). The school should receive information on the money value of what it gets (norms para 135). A school with some but not all three functions is funded partly each way (norms para 138).

Example: a non-section 21 school needs Grade 4 readers. It submits its requisition to the district by the provincial deadline. It does not order from a bookshop and send the invoice later.

## 🆕 BELA: central buying of learning materials

BELA added s21(3A) (BELA s14). Despite a school's s21(1)(c) function, the HOD may, in consultation with the governing body, centrally procure identified learning and teaching support material, on the basis of efficient, effective and economic use of public funds or uniform norms and standards. A governing body may still buy those materials from a supplier if that is more cost effective, but it must give the HOD documentary proof that its own purchase will be cheaper than the central procurement.

> ⚠️ Watch out: If your school wants to buy identified materials itself, keep comparable quotes and a written comparison against the department's price before you commit. Without that proof you cannot rely on the s21(3A) proviso.

## 🔙 Losing a function

The HOD may, on reasonable grounds, withdraw one or more functions. He or she must first give written notice with reasons, allow representations, consider them and give a written final decision (SASA s22(1) and (2), as substituted by BELA s15). In urgent cases the HOD may act first and follow these steps immediately afterwards (SASA s22(3)). Spending the allocation in ways that starve educational inputs is a reason the norms give for considering withdrawal (norms para 140).

## ✅ Key points

- Section 21(1)(a), (c) and (d) cover maintenance, learning materials and services (SASA s21(1)).
- Section 21 schools receive the money and procure themselves, keeping proof for audit (norms paras 132 and 133).
- Non-section 21 schools are supplied by the department up to the value of their allocation (norms para 135).
- Under BELA the HOD may centrally procure identified learning materials, and a school may buy them itself only with proof that it is cheaper (SASA s21(3A)).
- The HOD may withdraw functions after written notice and a chance to respond (SASA s22).

lessons.title: Fundraising, budgets, reporting and pitfalls
lessons.summary: Voluntary contributions, the budget and audit duties that still apply, and the mistakes that get no-fee schools into trouble.
lessons.body:
## 🤲 Raising extra money

No-fee status does not remove the governing body's duty to take all reasonable measures within its means to supplement state resources (SASA s36(1)). It may hold fundraising events, seek donations and sponsorships, and invite voluntary contributions from parents.

### 🚫 But nothing may be compulsory

- A no-fee school may not charge school fees (SASA s39(7); norms para 43).
- "School fees" includes any monetary contribution paid in relation to a learner's attendance or participation in any school programme (SASA s1). A compulsory "voluntary contribution", "development levy" or "trip fee" for an official programme is therefore a school fee in disguise.
- No learner may be refused admission over money, or be excluded from any part of the programme, or be denied a report or transfer certificate, because a parent did not pay (SASA s5(3)(a) and s41(7)).

> ⚠️ Watch out: A letter saying "every family must contribute R100 for the sports day" makes the payment compulsory. Say instead that contributions are welcome, voluntary, and that every learner takes part either way.

## 🏦 All money into the school fund

Donations, fundraising proceeds and voluntary contributions must be paid into the school fund and the school's one bank account (SASA s37(2) and (3)). Donations must be used according to their conditions (SASA s37(4)). A cash tin kept by a staff member for the tuck shop is outside the school fund and a common audit finding.

Business activities on school property to raise money need MEC approval (SASA s36(4)(a)(ii)), and the State is not liable for losses from such an enterprise or if s36(2) was not followed (SASA s60(4), as amended by BELA s38).

## 📝 Budgeting still applies

Every public school, no-fee or not, must prepare a budget each year and present it to a general meeting of parents on at least 30 days' notice (SASA s38(1) and (2)). BELA's rules apply in full: the budget and an explanation are sent to parents and open for inspection 14 days before, a 10 per cent quorum applies, and deviations of 10 per cent or more or reallocations need a further parents' meeting (SASA s38(3) to (7), as amended by BELA s28). Build the budget around the allocation letter and the province's recommended breakdown.

## 📊 Reporting and audit

The same duties apply as in a fee-paying school:

- Keep full records and draw up annual financial statements within three months after year end, then present them to parents with 14 days' inspection notice (SASA s42, as substituted by BELA s31).
- Have them audited by a registered auditor, or examined if an audit is not reasonably practicable, by someone with no financial interest in the school (SASA s43(1) to (3)).
- Send quarterly income and expenditure reports within 30 days after each quarter, and the audited or examined statements within six months after year end, to the HOD (SASA s43(5), as substituted by BELA s32).
- Section 21 schools must also keep procurement documents for audit (norms para 133).

> 💡 Tip: Ask the district whether the province offers or pays for examiners for small no-fee schools. Practice differs by province.

## 🧨 Common pitfalls

1. Paying a cleaner or assistant teacher from the state allocation. It may not pay personnel (norms para 99).
2. Building a classroom with the allocation. New buildings are excluded (norms para 99).
3. Making "voluntary" contributions compulsory, or keeping lists of non-payers (SASA s1 and s41(7)).
4. Signing a lease for a printer without the HOD's written approval (SASA s36(2)).
5. Under-spending on learning materials without the department's approval (norms para 140).
6. Missing the 30-day quarterly report deadline (SASA s43(5)(a)).
7. A member voting on a contract with a relative's business without declaring and recusing (SASA s26).

## ✅ Key points

- Fundraising is allowed and expected, but every contribution must be truly voluntary (SASA s36(1), s1 and s39(7)).
- All money, including donations, goes into the school fund (SASA s37(2)).
- Budget, parents' meeting, records, audit and quarterly reports apply to no-fee schools too (SASA s38, s42 and s43).
- The allocation never pays for staff or new buildings (norms para 99).

questions.text: Who determines each year which national quintiles must be used to identify schools that may not charge fees?

options.text: The governing body, at the budget meeting
The Minister, by notice in the Government Gazette
The district director
The school principal

questions.explanation: SASA s39(7) requires the Minister to determine annually, by notice in the Government Gazette, the quintiles or parts of quintiles used to identify no-fee schools.

questions.text: Under the norms, what two conditions make a school a no-fee school?

options.text: It has fewer than 500 learners and is in a rural area
Its parents vote against fees and the SGB agrees
It is in a quintile identified by the Minister and receives at least the no fee threshold per learner
It has section 21 status and a clean audit

questions.explanation: Paragraph 156 of the Amended National Norms and Standards for School Funding (2006) sets both criteria, read with SASA s39(7) and (8).

questions.text: A no-fee school receives less per learner than the no fee threshold. What may it do?

options.text: Charge school fees up to the difference between the threshold and what it received
Charge the same fees as a nearby fee-paying school
Nothing at all, under any circumstances
Charge a registration fee instead

questions.explanation: SASA s39(11) and (12) allow such a school to charge fees limited to the threshold minus the actual state amount received. Registration fees are banned by s39(5).

questions.text: Which of these may the state school allocation NOT be used for?

options.text: Electricity and water accounts
Library books
Repairs to a broken window
The salary of an SGB-employed assistant teacher

questions.explanation: Paragraph 99 of the norms says the school allocation may not be used to cover the cost of personnel and new buildings. Services, learning materials and repairs are listed in para 96.

questions.text: Which section 21 function covers buying textbooks and educational equipment?

options.text: Section 21(1)(a)
Section 21(1)(b)
Section 21(1)(c)
Section 21(1)(d)

questions.explanation: SASA s21(1)(c) is the function to purchase textbooks, educational materials or equipment. (a) is maintenance, (b) is extramural curriculum and subject choice, (d) is paying for services.

questions.text: A school does NOT have section 21 functions. How does it usually get learning materials?

options.text: The department procures them up to the value of the school's allocation
The principal buys them and claims the money back
Parents must buy them
The school may not receive any learning materials

questions.explanation: Paragraph 135 of the norms describes the common approach of provincial departments procuring resources in bulk for non-section 21 schools relative to their allocations.

questions.text: Under BELA, the HOD centrally procures identified learning materials. When may a section 21 school buy them itself instead?

options.text: Whenever the SGB prefers a local supplier
Never, once the HOD has decided to procure centrally
Only if parents approve it at a general meeting
When it is more cost effective and the SGB gives the HOD documentary proof of that

questions.explanation: SASA s21(3A), inserted by BELA s14, allows the governing body to buy from a supplier only where that is more cost effective, and it must give the HOD documentary proof.

questions.text: A no-fee school sends a letter saying every family must pay R100 towards the sports day. Why is this unlawful?

options.text: Sports days may only be funded by the department
A compulsory payment for participation in a school programme is a school fee, which a no-fee school may not charge
The amount is too high
Only the principal may sign letters about money

questions.explanation: SASA s1 defines school fees to include any monetary contribution paid in relation to participation in any school programme, and a no-fee school may not charge school fees (SASA s39(7)).

questions.text: Must a no-fee school hold a parents' meeting to approve its budget?

options.text: No, because the state allocation is fixed by the department
Only if it raises more than 10 per cent of its income from donations
Yes, every public school must present its budget to a general meeting of parents
Only in years when it changes section 21 status

questions.explanation: SASA s38(1) and (2) apply to every public school: the budget must be presented to a general meeting of parents on at least 30 days' notice.

questions.text: What must the HOD do before withdrawing a school's section 21 function, outside an urgent case?

options.text: Inform the SGB in writing with reasons, allow representations, consider them and give a written final decision
Obtain a court order
Hold a general meeting of parents
Nothing, the HOD may withdraw functions at any time

questions.explanation: SASA s22(1) and (2), as substituted by BELA s15, require reasonable grounds, written notice with reasons, a chance to make representations, due consideration and a written final decision.
